The current form of schooling—in which children of the same age gather in one classroom and are taught by a teacher—began in the nineteenth century. Before that time, even when children studied together in one room, their learning content was individualized, and their ages varied. This was because each child needed different knowledge. AI (artificial intelligence) is being used in many fields. Typical examples include predicting when and where traffic congestion will occur and checking whether old bridges and roads are dangerous—that is, carrying out regular inspections. Normally, people inspect things by looking at them directly, then touching or tapping areas that appear problematic to investigate them in detail. Now, however, AI is being used for this work. It is said that if people provide examples and train AI, it will be able to work accurately without making any mistakes.
Using cameras is also highly effective. When a camera mounted on a car records the condition of a road surface, AI examines the images and identifies problematic locations. In recent years, festivals have become very popular. Even tourists can feel as though they are participating simply by being there, enjoy the traditional atmosphere, and sample food from the street stalls. As images of festivals spread on social media, not only famous festivals but also traditional festivals in small towns have begun to attract attention.
The town of Yamada ① is also one of the towns that continues to hold such a festival.
It is good that festivals are popular. The number of visitors to local shops increases, bringing economic benefits. The people of Yamada, which had maintained its festival for many years, ②used to think so. However, this year, a small bridge collapsed in one town because too many people gathered, forcing the festival to be canceled. In another town, waste and safety problems became serious, and there were reportedly complaints from visitors. One town spent considerable time and money preparing, but contrary to expectations, only negative reports spread. As a result, opinions that the festival ③should be discontinued have begun to appear in Yamada. The number of towns like this is increasing.

If not only the core organizers but also children and new residents participate, their sense of connection as town residents will grow stronger, and their desire to “build a better town together” will increase. Isn't that the most important thing for a town? Rather than holding a festival for tourists, wouldn't it be better to return to holding one for ourselves?

When I had just joined the company, whenever there was a drinking party, my seniors would ask me things like, “What do you like to eat?” and “What restaurant would be good?” Since I knew nothing, I always said, “I’ll leave it up to you” or “Whatever you think is best.” That was because I believed that whatever my seniors chose could not possibly be wrong.
However, recently, when I found myself in the position of asking someone else, I finally understood. Hearing “It’s up to you” is actually a great deal of pressure. Even when the person asking receives that answer, they do not get the information they need to reach a decision, leaving them in an extremely awkward position. Since I used to give exactly the same answer, I realized that I must have caused trouble for my seniors. If I were in that situation now, I would never answer that way again.
Moreover, I realized that people differ in how they use and interpret this expression. I used it because I thought the other person would be pleased to think, “They trust me, so they are leaving the decision to me,” but apparently some people become angry, thinking, “This person has no intention of giving a proper answer to my question.” What surprised me was that some people use the expression to mean, “I don’t have time to think and I’m not confident, so I’m asking you to choose for me—but you had better choose something I’ll be satisfied with.” People like this sometimes later say things such as, “It would have been better if you hadn’t chosen this.” The person who hears that would surely want to shout angrily, “Weren’t you the one who said it was up to me?!”

After entering university, I joined a hospital volunteer program (Note 1), which gave me more opportunities to talk with sick people. As a result, I wanted to learn more about health. Being famous is truly difficult. When I see reports saying, "The child of that celebrity was arrested by the police. The parents are at fault for failing to raise the child properly," followed by the celebrity being dragged in front of television cameras and forced to apologize publicly, I think this. If the celebrity themselves were criticized for doing something wrong, that would be understandable. However, if their child commits an offense serious enough to be arrested, is it entirely the parents’ fault?

From an academic perspective, the part of a child’s development that parents can control appears to be quite small. According to one study, a child’s personality seems to be determined largely by inborn factors and relationships with childhood friends. This is deeply connected to the way people have lived since ancient times. In the past, when a mother gave birth to another child, older children left their parents and grew up with the mutual help of their siblings and the children around them. For a child to grow up, being accepted by peers—in other words, friends—was more important than anything else. Because of this history, children are influenced more by their friends than by their parents.

However, in general, rather than listening to scientific explanations like this, it is much more entertaining to assume that a celebrity is a bad person and have everyone criticize them together. Since condemning "bad behavior" is a "good deed," people can loudly voice their criticism. Such television programs are enjoyable to watch, so they become popular, and the broadcasters make a great deal of money.

The mass media, such as television, value presenting incidents in a sensational and entertaining way to amuse people more than communicating the truth accurately. We must not forget this.

A certain company placed an advertisement that read: “① Please allow us to place video cameras in your home for one month. We will give you 200,000 yen as a token of our appreciation.” Several video cameras would be installed in the home, and recording would also take place (note). However, as long as you stayed at home for 8 hours each day, you could spend the rest of the time outside.
The company apparently placed the advertisement to investigate whether data recording people’s daily lives could be bought and sold. It seems to be planning to remove personally identifying information from the collected lifestyle data in the future before selling it or making it available for viewing on the internet.
The purchase of these videos has received both support and opposition. Supporters say it is a good idea because people can ② earn money easily without having to work. Those who do not want to work, as well as those who want to work but are unable to, would not have to face having no income.
On the other hand, opponents argue that using video cameras in this way is extremely dangerous. For example, passwords could be identified from the movements of a person’s fingers while using a computer, and personal information could be exposed through things the person never even notices.
Nevertheless, many businesses collect and buy and sell lifestyle data without our knowledge. Stores record customers’ ages and genders along with the items they purchased. In addition, simply by using the internet, information such as our location and the things we have bought is collected. Yet the people whose data is collected are completely unaware of it. Considering these facts, it can be said that company ③, which pays people properly in this way, is more honest and commendable.
(Note) 録画 (video recording): The act of recording with a video camera.
